b.7909d2b3.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.7909d2b3.t: Look at Figure 1. Why does the right side of the heart send blood to the lungs first?
tieu_chi: Says the blood goes to the lungs to pick up oxygen (because it has little / no oxygen); saying it needs to get oxygen is enough. Getting rid of carbon dioxide is a bonus, not required.
mau: The blood in the right side of the heart is deoxygenated. It goes to the lungs first to pick up oxygen and get rid of carbon dioxide.

b.2c4f7a6b.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.2c4f7a6b.t: Trace a drop of blood from the right side of the heart to the left side of the heart.
tieu_chi: The blood goes from the right side of the heart to the lungs.
In the lungs the blood picks up oxygen (becomes oxygenated).
Then the blood goes back to the left side of the heart. The order must be right; RA, RV, LA, LV are fine but not required.
mau: The blood leaves the right side of the heart and goes to the lungs. In the lungs it picks up oxygen. Then it goes back to the left side of the heart.

b.91a0f517.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.91a0f517.t: What happens to the oxygen in the blood when it goes through the lungs?
tieu_chi: Says the blood picks up / takes in oxygen in the lungs (the blood gets more oxygen). A short sentence is enough.
mau: In the lungs, oxygen from the air goes into the blood, so the blood gets more oxygen (it becomes oxygenated).

b.21cddae6.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.21cddae6.t: How is a bird's heart system like a human's heart system?
tieu_chi: Gives one correct way they are alike: four chambers / a left and a right side, OR blood goes to the lungs and then to the body. A short sentence is enough.
mau: Like a human heart, a bird's heart has four parts (two sides). It pumps blood to the lungs and then to the rest of the body.

b.d39d725f.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.d39d725f.t: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
tieu_chi: Says the muscles / body need more oxygen (or energy) when you run.
Explains the heart beats faster to send more blood with oxygen to them.
mau: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen. Your heart beats faster to pump more blood with oxygen to the muscles.

b.aed8a5f3.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.aed8a5f3.t: Why is the heart called a 'pump'?
tieu_chi: Says the heart pushes / moves blood through the body. A short sentence is enough.
mau: The heart is called a pump because it pushes blood around the whole body.

b.e5357c8c.t: Choose one system from the glossary above. Why is this system important for the human body?
tieu_chi: Names one body system.
Gives the main job of that system correctly (circulatory: moves blood with oxygen and nutrients; respiratory: takes in oxygen, gets rid of carbon dioxide; reproductive: makes offspring).
mau: I choose the circulatory system. It is important because it carries oxygen and nutrients to all parts of the body.
The respiratory system is important because it takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

b.bb83d8b5.yeu_cau: Directions: Choose one body system from the matching activity. Use the sentence frames below to explain why that system is important for the body.
b.bb83d8b5.t: I am choosing the ___ system. The _ system is important because it __.
tieu_chi: Fills in the same body system name in both blanks.
The 'because it ...' part gives the main job of that system correctly.
mau: I am choosing the circulatory system. The circulatory system is important because it pumps blood to carry oxygen around the body.
I am choosing the respiratory system. The respiratory system is important because it takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

b.fc97e34e.yeu_cau: Fill in the blanks and answer the questions about how your body systems help each other.
b.fc97e34e.t: Why do the heart and lungs need to work together when you exercise?
tieu_chi: Says the muscles / body need more oxygen when you exercise.
Says the lungs take in the oxygen (you breathe faster).
Says the heart pumps the blood that carries the oxygen to the muscles (beats faster).
mau: When you exercise, your muscles need more oxygen. The lungs take in more oxygen, and the heart pumps blood faster to carry that oxygen to the muscles.

b.9f933c0f.t: 2. Write down the function of 1, 2 and 6?
tieu_chi: Number 1 = nasal cavity (or nose): where air first comes in (mucus traps dust is a bonus).
Number 2 = mouth: air goes in and out through it.
Number 6 = diaphragm: the muscle under the lungs that helps us breathe in and out.
mau: 1 is the nasal cavity: air first enters here, and mucus traps dirt and dust. 2 is the mouth: air can go in and out through it. 6 is the diaphragm: the muscle under the lungs that controls breathing.

b.ef183d83.yeu_cau: Label the diagram, and explain the 2 (two) processes shown the diagram
b.ef183d83.t: Label the diagram, and explain the 2 (two) processes shown the diagram
tieu_chi: Names the two processes: breathing in (inhaling) and breathing out (exhaling).
Inhaling: air goes in and the lungs / chest get bigger (diaphragm moves down).
Exhaling: air goes out and the lungs / chest get smaller (diaphragm moves up).
Labels are not needed; only the explanation is marked.
mau: The first picture shows inhaling: air goes in through the nose, the diaphragm moves down and the lungs get bigger. The second picture shows exhaling: the diaphragm moves up, the lungs get smaller and air is pushed out.

b.d5127238.t: What are the functions and structure of lungs?
tieu_chi: Function: the lungs move oxygen into the blood.
Function: the lungs remove carbon dioxide from the blood (we breathe it out).
Structure: says something correct about how lungs are built (two lungs inside the rib cage, air tubes / bronchi, air sacs / alveoli).
mau: The lungs are inside the rib cage. They take oxygen from the air into the blood and remove carbon dioxide from the blood. They are full of small air tubes and tiny air sacs.

b.7a05eafd.t: What is the work of the sheet of muscle?
tieu_chi: Says it helps us breathe / helps the lungs move (makes the lungs bigger and smaller). A short sentence is enough.
mau: The sheet of muscle (the diaphragm) helps the lungs move so that we can breathe in and out.

b.43337449.t: How does the sheet of muscle move?
tieu_chi: Says it moves down and up (it contracts and relaxes). A short phrase is enough.
mau: The sheet of muscle moves down and up.

b.a9e9b2fb.t: Can you guess what happens to the sheet of muscle when we breath in or out?
tieu_chi: Breathing in: the muscle moves down (flattens) and the lungs get bigger.
Breathing out: the muscle moves up (curves) and the lungs get smaller.
mau: When we breathe in, the sheet of muscle moves down and the lungs get bigger. When we breathe out, it moves up and the lungs get smaller.

b.ca30b73a.yeu_cau: A scientist carried out a study with 100 girls to find out the age at which they started puberty. This a graph of her findings.
b.ca30b73a.t: Describe three signs in girls that puberty has started.
tieu_chi: Gives three different signs that puberty has started in girls.
Each sign is one of: grows taller; skin becomes oily; more body hair grows; breasts develop; hips get wider; voice gets a little deeper.
If the learner gives menstruation as a sign, it does not count as one of the three; the feedback explains that it usually begins about a year after puberty starts.
mau: Any three from: grows taller; skin becomes oily, more body hair grows, breasts develop; hips get wider; voice gets a little deeper. Note that menstruation usually begins about a year after the start of puberty.

b.3205d28c.t: Name one physical change that happens to BOTH boys and girls during puberty, and one change that is different for each.
tieu_chi: Names one change that happens to both boys and girls: grow taller, grow body hair or get oily skin.
Names a change that is different for each: for boys, the voice deepens or the shoulders broaden; for girls, the hips widen or menstruation begins.
A change for boys only and a change for girls only are both given; a short phrase for each is enough.
mau: Both boys and girls grow taller. Boys' voices deepen and girls' hips widen.
Both boys and girls get oily skin. Boys' shoulders broaden, and girls begin menstruation.
b.3205d28c.bai_doc:
Puberty: Physical Changes — Growing and changing

During puberty, boys and girls go through many physical changes as their bodies grow. Both boys and girls grow taller, grow body hair, and get oily skin. There are also changes that are different for each. Boys' voices deepen and their shoulders broaden. Girls' hips widen and they begin menstruation. These changes are a natural part of growing up.

b.5b26e42c.yeu_cau: Malaria is a serious disease that kills millions of people around the world each year. The table shows the number of malaria cases reported at a clinic in Indonesia in one year.
b.5b26e42c.t: Describe three things that people can do to help prevent getting diseases such as malaria.
tieu_chi: Gives three different ways to prevent getting malaria.

Each way stops mosquito bites or reduces the number of mosquitoes, for example: sleep under bed nets; wear long sleeves and long pants; keep doors and windows closed at night; use insect repellent; burn mosquito coils; empty standing water; spray insecticide.
mau:
Any three from:
• sleep under bed nets
• wear long sleeves and long pants
• keep doors and windows closed at night when mosquitoes are active
• use insect repellents on their skin to keep insects away
• burn mosquito coils to keep insects away

b.afba4249.yeu_cau: More Science Topics: Research, Data, and Staying Safe
b.afba4249.t: List two ways a person can prevent being bitten by insects (for example, when playing outside or camping).
tieu_chi: Gives two different ways to avoid insect bites, for example: wear long sleeves and long pants; use insect repellent; sleep under a bed net; keep doors and windows closed; burn mosquito coils.
A short phrase for each way is enough.
mau: Wear long sleeves and long pants, and use insect repellent on your skin.
Sleep under a bed net and burn mosquito coils.

b.e35235c6.yeu_cau: Marcus measured his pulse rate while he was sitting still and then after doing different types of physical activities. These are his results.
b.e35235c6.t: When was Marcus’s pulse rate lowest? Explain why.
tieu_chi: Says that the pulse rate was lowest when Marcus was sitting still.
Explains why: the body needs less food and oxygen when it is still, so the heart does not have to beat fast.
mau: Marcus’s pulse rate was lowest when he was sitting still. The body needs less food and oxygen when it is still or inactive, so the heart does not have to beat fast.

b.a48ce67d.yeu_cau: Marcus measured his pulse rate while he was sitting still and then after doing different types of physical activities. These are his results.
b.a48ce67d.t: Is there a measurement that needs to be checked? If so, which one and why?
tieu_chi: Says yes and names the digging result (80 heartbeats per minute).
Explains why: the pulse rate is low for a physical activity; we would expect it to be higher.
mau: Yes. The measurement for digging. The pulse rate measured is low although he is doing a physical activity. We would expect the measurement to be higher.

b.b72d3f58.yeu_cau: Marcus measured his pulse rate while he was sitting still and then after doing different types of physical activities. These are his results.
b.b72d3f58.t: Explain how Marcus could make this a fair test.
tieu_chi: Gives a way to make the test fair: do every activity for the same length of time before measuring, OR rest (sit still) before each activity so the heartbeat returns to normal.
One of these two ideas is enough.
mau: He should do all the activities for the same length of time, then measure his pulse rate. He should also start each activity after a period of rest (sitting still) to allow his heartbeat to return to normal.

b.64d65d71.yeu_cau: Marcus measured his pulse rate while he was sitting still and then after doing different types of physical activities. These are his results.
b.64d65d71.t: Write a conclusion for Marcus’s findings.
tieu_chi: States the link: more physical activity / exercise makes the pulse rate increase.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Body activity/exercise makes the pulse rate increase.

b.3e2b45ca.yeu_cau: Marcus measured his pulse rate while he was sitting still and then after doing different types of physical activities. These are his results.
b.3e2b45ca.t: Predict how Marcus’s pulse rate would change if he pedalled faster on the bicycle. Explain your answer.
tieu_chi: Predicts that the pulse rate would increase (go up).
Explains why: when you are more active, the heart must beat more often to carry enough food and oxygen in the blood to the muscles.
mau: Marcus’s pulse rate would increase. The more active you are, i.e. pedalling faster, the more often your heart must beat to carry enough food and oxygen from the blood to your muscles.

b.9b2d8c41.yeu_cau: Class 5 measured the pulse rate and breathing rate of 10 people after they had jogged on the spot for three minutes. Here are their results.
b.9b2d8c41.t: Describe the pattern you observe in the results.
tieu_chi: Describes the pattern: the higher the pulse rate, the higher the breathing rate (both go up together).
A short phrase is enough.
mau: As the pulse rate increase, the breathing rate also increases during exercise OR The higher the pulse rate, the higher the breathing rate.

b.b0a3d68a.yeu_cau: Class 5 measured the pulse rate and breathing rate of 10 people after they had jogged on the spot for three minutes. Here are their results.
b.b0a3d68a.t: Suggest a conclusion that class 5 can make from these results.
tieu_chi: Gives a conclusion that links the two: after jogging, a person with a higher breathing rate has a higher pulse rate than a person with a lower breathing rate.
mau: After jogging on the spot for three minutes, a person with a high breathing rate has a higher pulse rate than a person with a low breathing rate.

b.593bd95c.yeu_cau: Class 5 measured the pulse rate and breathing rate of 10 people after they had jogged on the spot for three minutes. Here are their results.
tieu_chi: Gives one sensible reason for the odd result, for example: the breathing rate was not measured accurately, or the person has a very large lung capacity.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Learners’ own suggestions, for example, the breathing rate was not accurately measured, or the person had a very large lung capacity.
b.593bd95c.bai_doc:
Question 4c (i)

Identify any results that do not fit the pattern.
The person with a pulse rate of 100 heartbeats per minute and a breathing rate of 26 breaths per minute.

b.8b2d3bd2.yeu_cau: A scientist carried out a study with 100 girls to find out the age at which they started puberty. This a graph of her findings.
b.8b2d3bd2.t: Suggest a factor that affects the age at which puberty starts.
tieu_chi: Suggests one reasonable factor, e.g. body mass (the table shows girls start puberty at about the same average mass, 45 to 47 kg). A short phrase is enough.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Body mass
b.8b2d3bd2.bai_doc:
Mass of the girls at the start of puberty

The scientist also measured the mass of the girls at the start of puberty. This is a summary of her results.

b.989a1d98.yeu_cau: A scientist carried out a study with 100 girls to find out the age at which they started puberty. This a graph of her findings.
b.989a1d98.t: What pattern can you see in the results?
tieu_chi: States the pattern: puberty starts when girls have about the same average mass, 45 to 47 kg, whatever their age.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Puberty starts when girls have an average mass of 45 to 47 kg.
b.989a1d98.bai_doc:
Mass of the girls at the start of puberty

The scientist also measured the mass of the girls at the start of puberty. This is a summary of her results.

b.adf1269a.yeu_cau: A scientist carried out a study with 100 girls to find out the age at which they started puberty. This a graph of her findings.
b.adf1269a.t: In the past, most girls started puberty at about the age of 14. Suggest a reason why puberty starts at a younger age.
tieu_chi: Gives a reason: better nutrition / more food.
Explains the link: girls grow faster, so their mass increases sooner and they reach puberty earlier.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Better nutrition/more food makes girls grow faster, so their mass increases and they reach puberty earlier.
b.adf1269a.bai_doc:
Mass of the girls at the start of puberty

The scientist also measured the mass of the girls at the start of puberty. This is a summary of her results.

b.9164dfde.yeu_cau: Malaria is a serious disease that kills millions of people around the world each year. The table shows the number of malaria cases reported at a clinic in Indonesia in one year.
b.9164dfde.t: Suggest reason for this pattern in the data
tieu_chi: Links the data to the seasons: the most cases are in the wet season (November to March) and the fewest in the dry season (April to October).
Gives a reason: mosquitoes breed in the wet season, so there are more mosquitoes to spread malaria.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: The fewest cases occurred in the dry season and the most cases in the wet season. Mosquitoes breed in the wet season (or similar answer).
b.9164dfde.bai_doc:
Climate in Indonesia

Indonesia has a warm tropical climate with a dry season from April to October, and a wet monsoon season from November to March.

b.f1dfafa6.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.f1dfafa6.t: Look at the table. What happens to the pulse rate as an animal gets bigger?
tieu_chi: Says the pulse rate goes down (decreases / gets slower) as the animal gets bigger.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: The pulse rate gets lower as an animal gets bigger.
It decreases.

b.45c4d6b5.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.45c4d6b5.t: Why should you check your pulse three times instead of just once?
tieu_chi: Says that repeating makes the result more accurate / reliable, OR that one measurement could be a mistake.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Checking three times makes the result more reliable, because one measurement could be a mistake.
So you can spot a wrong result and work out an average.

b.65122332.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.65122332.t: Plan a fair test to see how exercise changes pulse rate. What do you change (independent variable) and what do you measure (dependent variable)?
tieu_chi: Independent variable: what you change is the exercise (rest compared with exercise, or the type / amount of exercise).
Dependent variable: what you measure is the pulse rate (beats per minute).
mau: I change how much exercise I do (resting or running). I measure the pulse rate.
The independent variable is the exercise (rest, walking or running); the dependent variable is the pulse rate in beats per minute.

b.5e19d6d6.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.5e19d6d6.t: Why do we use drawings to study the heart and blood?
tieu_chi: Gives a reason: we cannot see the heart and blood inside the body, so a drawing / diagram shows the parts and how blood moves.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: We cannot see inside the body, so drawings show us the parts of the heart and how blood moves.
Drawings show the heart and blood vessels clearly, because we cannot look inside a living body.

b.8253ab78.yeu_cau: Read each question and look at the pictures to help you.
b.8253ab78.t: What will happen to a person's pulse if they sit and rest for 10 minutes after running?
tieu_chi: Says the pulse rate goes down / slows down (back towards the normal resting rate).
A short phrase is enough.
mau: The pulse rate will slow down and go back to the resting pulse rate.
It will go down.

b.ba046b3a.t: What is the independent variable (the thing Jada changes) in this experiment?
tieu_chi: Names what Jada changes: exercise, that is running (or sitting still versus running).
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Exercise (running).
b.ba046b3a.bai_doc:
The Experiment

Jada wants to know how exercise affects heart rate. She measures her heart rate while sitting still. Then, she runs for 5 minutes and measures her heart rate again. She repeats this for three days to make sure her results are accurate. [Steps of the Experiment: Resting Heart Rate → Exercise (Running) → Active Heart Rate → Compare Results]

b.8f64c820.t: Describe one way Jada keeps this a fair test.
tieu_chi: Names one thing Jada keeps the same: she runs for 5 minutes each time, the same person (Jada) is tested, or she measures her heart rate the same way.
Repeating the test for three days to check the results is also accepted.
mau: Jada runs for the same time, 5 minutes, every time.
She measures her own heart rate in the same way each day.

b.eac8bcd1.t: Make a prediction. What do you think will happen to Jada's heart rate after she runs?
tieu_chi: Predicts that Jada's heart rate will increase (be higher / faster) after running.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Her heart rate will be higher after she runs.
I think her heart rate will go up.

b.3863a007.t: In your own words, what does it mean to do research? Why do scientists do research before an experiment?
tieu_chi: Explains research in own words: finding out information carefully (asking questions, observing, using books or experts).
Gives a reason why scientists research before an experiment, e.g. to learn what is already known, to plan the experiment well, or to make a good prediction.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Research means finding out information carefully from books, experts or by observing. Scientists do research first so they know what is already known and can plan a good experiment.
b.3863a007.bai_doc:
Key Terms: Research

Research — finding out information carefully by asking questions, observing, and using reliable sources like books or experts.

b.eb1aca53.t: Maya measured her pulse 3 times after jumping rope: 120 bpm, 118 bpm, and 95 bpm. Which result is anomalous? What should Maya do with it, and why?
tieu_chi: Names 95 bpm as the anomalous result.
Says what to do: repeat the measurement, or leave it out (do not use it).
Explains why: it does not fit the pattern of the other results / it is much lower, so it may be a mistake.
mau: 95 bpm is anomalous. Maya should measure her pulse again because it does not fit the pattern and may be a mistake.
The anomalous result is 95 bpm. She should leave it out of her average because it is very different from 120 and 118.
b.eb1aca53.bai_doc:
Key Terms: Anomalous Results

Anomalous result — a result that does not fit the pattern of the other results. It is an "odd one out."

b.4b357aad.yeu_cau: Use these sentence frames to help explain your data:
b.4b357aad.t: Jada's heart rate was 70 beats per minute (bpm) at rest and 130 bpm after running. Use the words INCREASE or DECREASE to write one sentence explaining her results.
tieu_chi: Uses the word increase (increased) correctly: Jada's heart rate went up.
Links the change to running / exercise (from resting to after running); the numbers are not needed.
mau: Jada's heart rate increased from 70 bpm to 130 bpm after running.
When Jada ran, her heart rate increased.

b.88be9d99.yeu_cau: Use these sentence frames to help explain your data:
b.88be9d99.t: Look at the bar graph above. Which bar is taller, and what does that tell you about Jada's heart rate?
tieu_chi: Says the After Running bar is taller.
Says what it means: Jada's heart rate was higher (faster) after running than when resting.
mau: The After Running bar is taller, so Jada's heart rate was higher after running than at rest.

As ___ increased, ___ increased/decreased. When ___ decreased, ___ ...

b.7eeb9e67.t: List two safety rules you should follow while exercising (for example: warm up first, stay hydrated, wear proper shoes, stop if you feel pain or dizziness).
tieu_chi: Gives two different safety rules for exercising, for example: warm up first; stay hydrated; wear proper shoes; stop if you feel pain or dizziness.
A short phrase for each rule is enough; the rules may be copied from the examples.
mau: Warm up first and drink water to stay hydrated.
Wear proper shoes, and stop if you feel pain or dizziness.

b.91ab23f1.yeu_cau: Different liquids boil at different temperatures. Explain why this is so.
tieu_chi: Says boiling point is a property of a substance: each substance has its own boiling point.
Explains that the liquids are different substances, so they boil at different temperatures.
mau: Boiling point is a property of a substance, so different substances will have different boiling points.

b.4ed6f321.yeu_cau: Look at the pictures of beakers of water in a classroom.
b.4ed6f321.t: Write down one thing that is the same about the two processes.
tieu_chi: Says that in both processes liquid water changes into a gas (water vapour). A short phrase is enough.
mau: In both processes liquid water changes into water vapor gas.

b.5367de19.yeu_cau: Look at the pictures of beakers of water in a classroom.
b.5367de19.t: Write down two things that are different about the two processes.
tieu_chi: Gives two correct differences between boiling and evaporation.
Differences can be: boiling happens at 100 °C, evaporation at lower temperatures; in boiling bubbles of gas form all through the liquid, in evaporation there are no bubbles.
mau: Boiling happens when water is heated to 100 °C; evaporation happens at much lower temperatures; bubbles of gas form throughout the liquid in boiling, no bubbles form in evaporation.

b.bf8a9c58.yeu_cau: Look at the pictures of beakers of water in a classroom.
b.bf8a9c58.t: Explain the reason for your answer to 4b
tieu_chi: Says water boils at about 100 °C (boiling point is a property of water), so the boiling water in Beaker B is at about 100 °C.
mau: Boiling point is a property of a substance, and we know that water boils at around 100°C, or similar answer.

b.870dce72.yeu_cau: These are the boiling points of three liquids:
b.870dce72.t: Why is working with boiling oil more dangerous than working with boiling water?
tieu_chi: Says cooking oil boils at a much higher temperature than water (olive oil 300 °C, water 100 °C).
Explains that a burn from boiling oil would be much worse / more dangerous.
mau: Cooking oils boil at a much higher temperature than water. So, a burn from boiling oil will be much worse and more dangerous than a burn from boiling water.

b.678029dc.yeu_cau: Class 6 melted ice in a saucer and measured its temperature. These are their results.
b.678029dc.t: Do any other substances melt at this temperature? Say why or why not.
tieu_chi: Says no: other substances melt at different temperatures.
Explains that melting point is a property of a substance: each substance has its own melting point.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: No. Melting point is a property of a substance. Each substance has its own melting point, so other substances melt at different temperatures.

b.85b4779e.yeu_cau: Class 6 melted ice in a saucer and measured its temperature. These are their results.
b.85b4779e.t: Why does the ice on the saucer melt? Use the particle model to explain your answer.
tieu_chi: Says the ice takes in heat (thermal energy) from the warmer air around it.
Uses particles: the particles get more energy and move (vibrate) faster.
Says the particles break away from their fixed places and can move past each other, so the solid ice becomes liquid water.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: The ice takes in heat from the warmer air. Its particles get more energy and vibrate faster, until they break away from their fixed places and can move past each other. The solid ice becomes liquid water.

b.42d0e26f.yeu_cau: Mrs Kaur investigated boiling with her class. She heated water and measured its temperature. The class recorded these results.
b.42d0e26f.t: Suggest two ways you would know when the water boiled if you did not measure the temperature.
tieu_chi: Gives two signs that can be seen or heard, for example: big bubbles form all through the water; lots of steam rises; the water makes a bubbling sound.
A short phrase for each way is enough.
mau: I would see big bubbles of gas forming all through the water and rising to the top. I would also see lots of steam coming off the water.

b.be8f0eb6.yeu_cau: A. Definitions Write the meaning of each word.
tieu_chi: Says how hard a material is: how difficult it is to scratch, dent or change its shape. A short phrase is enough.
mau: Hardness is how hard a material is: how difficult it is to scratch or dent it.

b.3dfdf229.yeu_cau: A. Definitions Write the meaning of each word.
tieu_chi: Says whether / how easily a substance dissolves in a liquid such as water. A short phrase is enough.
mau: Solubility is how easily a substance dissolves in a liquid, such as water.

b.8bd2c60c.yeu_cau: A. Definitions Write the meaning of each word.
tieu_chi: Says it is the temperature at which a solid melts (changes into a liquid). A short phrase is enough.
mau: Melting point is the temperature at which a solid melts and changes into a liquid.

b.85804531.yeu_cau: A. Definitions Write the meaning of each word.
tieu_chi: Says how well a material lets electricity pass (flow) through it. A short phrase is enough.
mau: Electrical conductivity is how well a material lets electricity pass through it.

b.39bb38ea.yeu_cau: C. USE THE DATA Three substances have the following melting points:
b.39bb38ea.t: Why can melting point help scientists identify a substance?
tieu_chi: Says melting point is a property: each substance has its own (different) melting point.
Explains that measuring the melting point tells scientists which substance it is.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Melting point is a property of a substance. Each substance has its own melting point, so scientists can measure it to find out which substance it is.

b.2e3119cc.t: Why is knowing the properties of materials important when choosing materials to make objects?
tieu_chi: Says the properties tell us whether a material is suitable for the job the object must do.
Gives a reason or an example of what goes wrong with an unsuitable material (it could break, melt, let water in or burn your hand).
mau: We need to choose a material whose properties suit the job. For example, a saucepan handle should be a thermal insulator so it does not burn your hand.

b.5ace927c.yeu_cau: Explain why the properties of these materials make them suitable for their uses.
tieu_chi: Gives a property of glass that suits a window, for example: it is transparent (lets light through, you can see through it), waterproof or hard.
Links the property to the use: why it helps a window. A short sentence is enough.
mau: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see through the window. It is also waterproof, so it keeps the rain out.

b.28805898.yeu_cau: Explain why the properties of these materials make them suitable for their uses.
tieu_chi: Says copper is a good thermal (heat) conductor, so heat passes quickly to the food.
Another correct property (high melting point, strong, does not break) is a bonus, not required.
mau: Copper is a good thermal conductor, so heat passes quickly from the stove to the food. It also has a high melting point, so it does not melt.

b.e75c4d0b.yeu_cau: Write the meaning of these properties of materials.
tieu_chi: Says a permeable material lets water (or air) pass through it. A short phrase is enough.
mau: Permeable means a material lets water or air pass through it.

b.37dd4421.yeu_cau: Write the meaning of these properties of materials.
tieu_chi: Says an absorbent material soaks up (takes in) water. A short phrase is enough.
mau: Absorbent means a material can soak up water.

b.99a37510.yeu_cau: Give an example of when a material wouldn't be suitable for certain uses due to its properties.
tieu_chi: Names an object and a material that would not suit it.
Explains which property makes it unsuitable (for example, it melts, breaks, lets water through or conducts heat / electricity).
mau: A chocolate teapot would not be suitable. Chocolate has a low melting point, so it would melt when hot water is poured in.

tieu_chi: Says a gas has no fixed shape: it spreads out to fill its container (no fixed volume).
Particles far apart and moving fast is a bonus, not required.
mau: A gas has no fixed shape or volume. It spreads out to fill its container. Its particles are far apart and move quickly.

tieu_chi: Says a liquid takes the shape of its container / can flow or be poured. A short sentence is enough.
mau: A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape. It takes the shape of its container and can flow or be poured.

tieu_chi: Says a solid keeps its own fixed shape. A short sentence is enough.
mau: A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. Its particles are packed closely together.

b.b9644835.yeu_cau: Look at the picture of a lamp.
b.b9644835.t: Which parts of the lamp are electrical conductors?
tieu_chi: Names the metal parts as electrical conductors: the filament and the wires (the metal screw-in base and support wires also count).
Saying 'all the metal parts' is enough.
mau: All the metal parts: filament, wires, base

b.1cd70205.yeu_cau: Why are electrical plugs made of plastic?
tieu_chi: Says plastic is not an electrical conductor (it is an electrical insulator).
Explains that it protects you from an electric shock when you touch the plug.
mau: Plastic is not an electrical conductor. The plastic protects you from getting an electric shock when you touch the plug.

b.220b414b.yeu_cau: Why could your hand got burnt if you stirred hot soup with a metal spoon?
tieu_chi: Says metal is a good conductor of heat.
Explains that the spoon carries heat from the soup to your hand, so it could burn your hand.
mau: Metals are good conductors of heat. The metal spoon would conduct the heat from the soup to your hand, which could burn your hand.

b.b3cd4ff7.yeu_cau: Why is a wooden spoon good for stirring soup cooking in a pot?
tieu_chi: Says wood is not a good conductor of heat (it is a thermal insulator).
Explains that the spoon does not get hot, so it will not burn your hand.
mau: Wood is not a good conductor of heat, so the wooden spoon would not get hot and burn your hand.

b.d8978e26.yeu_cau: The table shows how well some common metals conduct heat. A high value means that the metal conducts heat very well.
b.d8978e26.t: Why do some cooking pots have a copper bottom?
tieu_chi: Says copper is a good heat (thermal) conductor.
Explains that heat moves quickly from the stove to the food in the pot.
mau: Copper is a good heat conductor, so it transfers heat from the stove quickly to the food in the pot.

b.4c9efca9.yeu_cau: The table shows how well some common metals conduct heat. A high value means that the metal conducts heat very well.
b.4c9efca9.t: Why do you think cooking pots are not made from silver?
tieu_chi: Says silver is much more expensive than copper.
Saying copper conducts heat almost as well as silver, so silver is not needed, is a bonus, not required.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Silver is much more expensive than copper, and copper is almost as good a heat conductor as silver.

b.bbcb352e.yeu_cau: The table shows how well some common metals conduct heat. A high value means that the metal conducts heat very well.
b.bbcb352e.t: Why are car radiators which cool the engine made from copper and brass?
tieu_chi: Says copper and brass are good heat conductors.
Explains that they carry heat away from the engine quickly, so it does not overheat.
mau: Copper and brass are good heat conductors, so they transfer heat away from the engine quickly to stop it overheating.

b.75308f5f.yeu_cau: Will a block of ice melt quicker in a plastic dish or a metal dish of the same size? Say why.
tieu_chi: Says the ice melts quicker in the metal dish.
Explains that metal is a better heat conductor than plastic, so heat moves into the ice faster.
mau: Ice will melt quicker in the metal dish. Metal is a better conductor of heat than plastic, so heat energy is transferred more quickly through the metal to the ice. This is why we saw the ice on the metal dish melt more quickly.

b.68d8915e.yeu_cau: If you touched a metal dish that contained an ice cube and a plastic dish that contained an ice cube, which dish would feel warmer? Say why.
tieu_chi: Says the plastic dish feels warmer.

Explains why: heat from the hand moves quickly into the metal (a good thermal conductor), so the metal feels cold, but slowly into the plastic (a poor thermal conductor). Explaining one dish is enough.
mau: The plastic dish will feel warmer. When you touch the metal dish, energy from your finger is conducted quickly into the metal. This lowers the temperature of your hand, so the metal feels cold.
Heat energy from your hand is conducted slowly into the plastic because it is not a good thermal conductor, so your hand does not cool quickly and you do not feel a lower temperature.

b.f1d7dbd5.t: Why are saucepan handles often made from plastic or wood instead of metal?
tieu_chi: Says plastic and wood are poor conductors of heat (thermal insulators).
Explains that the handle stays cool so it does not burn your hand (a metal handle would get hot).
mau: Plastic and wood are thermal insulators, so the handle does not get hot. A metal handle would conduct heat and burn your hand.

b.79d39bfb.t: A student puts a metal spoon and a wooden spoon into hot water. Which spoon would usually conduct thermal energy better? Why?
tieu_chi: Chooses the metal spoon.
Explains that metal is a good thermal conductor and wood is not (wood is a thermal insulator).
mau: The metal spoon would conduct thermal energy better. Metal is a good thermal conductor, but wood is a thermal insulator.

tieu_chi: Says metal is a good electrical conductor, so the metal disc is the best.
Says plastic (and wood) are electrical insulators: they do not let electricity pass through easily.
mau: The metal disc is the best conductor because metal is a good electrical conductor. Plastic and wood are electrical insulators, so electricity does not pass through them easily.

b.ae88d1a5.yeu_cau: PART 3: THINKING QUESTIONS (LEVEL 3) Answer the questions in full sentences.
b.ae88d1a5.t: A student wants to make a pan that can be used to cook food quickly and evenly. Which material would be the most suitable? (Choose from: plastic, wood, copper, glass) Explain your choice using at least two properties.
tieu_chi: Chooses copper.
Gives two properties of copper that make it suitable, for example: a good thermal (heat) conductor; a high melting point (it does not melt); strong (it does not break).
Links the properties to cooking food quickly and evenly.
mau: Copper is the most suitable. Copper is a good thermal conductor, so heat passes quickly and evenly to the food. It also has a high melting point, so it does not melt on the stove.

b.3d57191a.yeu_cau: The picture shows a test to find out about factors that affect dissolving.
b.3d57191a.t: Which factor that affects dissolving is being tested?
tieu_chi: Says the factor being tested is temperature: one beaker is heated and the other is not.
Naming the quantity of solute (as in the book answer) is also accepted.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: The quantity of solute, one beaker is heated and the other is not.

b.246ce55c.yeu_cau: The picture shows a test to find out about factors that affect dissolving.
b.246ce55c.t: Which factors are the same in both beakers?
tieu_chi: Names at least two factors that are the same: the quantity of water, the size and shape of the beaker, the material of the beaker.
mau: The quantity of water, the size and shape of the beaker, and the material that the beaker is made from.

b.328fa782.yeu_cau: The picture shows a test to find out about factors that affect dissolving.
b.328fa782.t: Which factors are different in the beakers?
tieu_chi: Names at least one factor that is different: the temperature (one beaker is heated) or the quantity of solute.
Naming stirring (as in the book answer) is also accepted.
mau: The quantity of solute and whether or not the solvent and solute is stirred.

b.be22ca49.yeu_cau: The picture shows a test to find out about factors that affect dissolving.
b.be22ca49.t: Will this be a fair test? Explain your answer.
tieu_chi: Says No.
Explains that more than one factor is different (the quantity of solute is different); in a fair test only the factor being tested is changed.
mau: No. The quantity of solute in the two beakers is different. In a fair test all factors must be the same except the factor being tested.

b.115dfe17.yeu_cau: Mrs Pather poured a cup of tea from the teapot and added two teaspoons of sugar and stirred the a few times. The tea was warm, not hot, so she drank it quickly. As she drank the last few drops, she noticed there was still sugar in the bottom of the cup.
b.115dfe17.t: Why was there still sugar at the bottom of the cup?
tieu_chi: Says the sugar had not all dissolved. A short sentence is enough.
mau: The sugar had not all dissolved.

b.e313c6ed.yeu_cau: Mrs Pather poured a cup of tea from the teapot and added two teaspoons of sugar and stirred the a few times. The tea was warm, not hot, so she drank it quickly. As she drank the last few drops, she noticed there was still sugar in the bottom of the cup.
b.e313c6ed.t: What two things could Mrs Pather have done do to make the all sugar dissolve?
tieu_chi: Gives two ways: stir the tea more, and heat the tea (make it hotter).
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: She could have stirred the tea more or heated it up.

b.90ce8c88.yeu_cau: Mrs Pather poured a cup of tea from the teapot and added two teaspoons of sugar and stirred the a few times. The tea was warm, not hot, so she drank it quickly. As she drank the last few drops, she noticed there was still sugar in the bottom of the cup.
b.90ce8c88.t: Use your knowledge about particles to explain how these two things help sugar dissolve faster.
tieu_chi: Explains stirring: it moves the solute (sugar) particles around so they spread into the spaces between the solvent (tea) particles.
Explains heating: it makes the particles move faster, so the sugar particles spread out more quickly.
mau: Stirring moves the particles of solute (sugar) around in the solvent (tea). This allows them to spread more easily into the spaces between the solvent (tea) particles.
Heating makes the particles of both solvent and solute move faster. This allows the solute particles to spread more easily into the spaces between the solvent particles until they are evenly spread.

b.c1da6e49.yeu_cau: Mrs Pather poured a cup of tea from the teapot and added two teaspoons of sugar and stirred the a few times. The tea was warm, not hot, so she drank it quickly. As she drank the last few drops, she noticed there was still sugar in the bottom of the cup.
b.c1da6e49.t: Predict what would happen to the sugar if Mrs Pather forgot to drink her cup of tea and left it standing for the whole afternoon.
tieu_chi: Predicts that all the sugar would dissolve (in the end).
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: The sugar would all dissolve.

b.8ef31bd4.yeu_cau: Mrs Pather poured a cup of tea from the teapot and added two teaspoons of sugar and stirred the a few times. The tea was warm, not hot, so she drank it quickly. As she drank the last few drops, she noticed there was still sugar in the bottom of the cup.
b.8ef31bd4.t: Use the particle model to explain your prediction.
tieu_chi: Says the particles of the sugar and the tea are always moving (bumping into each other).
Says the sugar particles spread out into the spaces between the tea particles until they are spread evenly.
Saying it happens slowly because the tea is not heated or stirred is a bonus, not required.
mau: The particles of both the solute (sugar) and solvent (tea) are constantly moving. This makes them bump into each other until they are eventually spread out evenly in the solution.
The solute particles can then fit into the spaces between the solvent particles and dissolve. This would happen slowly because the solution is not heated or stirred.

b.e07c3993.t: Give TWO examples of reversible changes.
tieu_chi: Gives two correct examples of reversible changes, e.g. melting ice, freezing water, melting chocolate, dissolving salt or sugar in water, evaporation, condensation.
The two examples must be different.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Melting ice and dissolving sugar in water are reversible changes.

b.0c8a8f4b.t: A learner says: “If a substance melts, it has become a new substance.” Do you agree? (Yes / No) Explain your answer.
tieu_chi: Says No (does not agree).
Explains that melting is only a change of state (solid to liquid); it is still the same substance, no new substance forms.
Saying it can be cooled / frozen back into a solid is also accepted as the explanation.
mau: No. When a substance melts it only changes state from solid to liquid. It is still the same substance and it can be cooled to become solid again.

b.9654b0e7.yeu_cau: Give an example of an irreversible change.
tieu_chi: Gives one correct irreversible change, e.g. burning wood or paper, cooking an egg, baking a cake, rusting.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Burning wood is an irreversible change.

b.afdb0da8.t: Why is melting ice a reversible change?
tieu_chi: Says the water can be frozen / cooled to turn back into ice.
Saying it is still the same substance (water) / no new substance forms is also accepted.
mau: Melting ice is reversible because the water can be frozen to become ice again. No new substance is made.

b.d746e214.t: A student says, "Evaporation is irreversible because the water disappears." Is the student correct? Explain.
tieu_chi: Says No (the student is not correct).
Explains the water changes into water vapour (a gas) that goes into the air; it does not disappear.
Says the water vapour can condense back into water, so evaporation is reversible.
mau: No. The water does not disappear. It changes into water vapour, a gas in the air. The water vapour can condense back into liquid water, so evaporation is reversible.

b.f9881ecc.yeu_cau: The drawing shows what happens when we mix iron and sulfur.
b.f9881ecc.t: Say why this is a chemical reaction.
tieu_chi: Says a new substance (product) forms. A short sentence is enough.
mau: A new substance or product forms.

b.2a6e2fc3.yeu_cau: Describe three ways we can tell if a chemical reaction has taken place.
tieu_chi: Describes three ways: a gas is produced (bubbles), there is a change of colour, there is a change in temperature.
A new substance forming (e.g. a solid, a smell or light) is also accepted as one way.
A short phrase for each way is enough.
mau: A gas is produced; there is a change of colour; there is a change in temperature.

b.aba24003.yeu_cau: When plants make food, they use carbon dioxide gas and water to form oxygen and a sugar called glucose. The picture shows a plant called pond weed.
b.aba24003.t: Suggest a way that we can obtain evidence that the chemical reaction has taken place.
tieu_chi: Says we can watch for bubbles of gas (oxygen) forming on the pond weed.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Observe bubbles of gas forming.

b.5667fca9.yeu_cau: When plants make food, they use carbon dioxide gas and water to form oxygen and a sugar called glucose. The picture shows a plant called pond weed.
b.5667fca9.t: Where do plants living on land get these reactants from?
tieu_chi: Says carbon dioxide comes from the air.
Says water comes from the soil (through the roots).
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Carbon dioxide comes from the air, water comes from the soil.

b.0b7272ba.yeu_cau: When plants make food, they use carbon dioxide gas and water to form oxygen and a sugar called glucose. The picture shows a plant called pond weed.
b.0b7272ba.t: Why is the chemical reaction described important for living things?
tieu_chi: Gives one reason: living things need the oxygen to stay alive / for respiration.
OR: animals cannot make their own food, so they eat plants (or animals that eat plants) to get energy.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Living things need oxygen gas to stay alive/for respiration; animals cannot make their own food, so they have to eat plants or other animals that eat plants in order to get their energy.

b.34c5e36d.yeu_cau: When plants make food, they use carbon dioxide gas and water to form oxygen and a sugar called glucose. The picture shows a plant called pond weed.
b.34c5e36d.t: Find out: any other factors that plants need for this process.
tieu_chi: Names sunlight (light).
Naming chlorophyll is a bonus, not required.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
A short phrase is enough.
mau: Sunlight, chlorophyll

b.8af60157.t: What evidence for a chemical reaction does the investigation show?
tieu_chi: Says the temperature changes / increases (it gets hotter). A short phrase is enough.

b.fd2e9484.yeu_cau: Plaster of Paris is a white powder that you mix with water. Doctors use it to help broken arms and legs grow back together properly. You can also make models with it. b.fd2e9484.t: Name two other types of evidence for a chemical reaction.
tieu_chi: Names two other types of evidence: gas bubbles form, a change in colour, a new substance forms.
A change in temperature does not count here (it is the one in the investigation).
A short phrase for each is enough.
mau: Gas bubbles form, and there is a change in colour.

b.da3d2140.yeu_cau: When we dissolve Epsom salts in water the temperature decreases.
b.da3d2140.t: Is the change in temperature evidence of a chemical reaction? Say why or why not.
tieu_chi: Says No.
Explains that no new substance forms: the Epsom salts only dissolve, and dissolving is a reversible change (we can get them back by evaporating the water).
mau: No. Dissolving Epsom salts in water is not a chemical reaction because no new substance forms. If the water evaporates, we get the Epsom salts back, so it is a reversible change.

mau: So that only the material changes. Then any change in the bulb is caused by the material, and the test is fair.

b.86394717.yeu_cau: Part D — Scientific Enquiry A student wants to find out which material is the best electrical conductor. They have: Copper, aluminium, plastic, rubber, a battery, wires, a bulb
b.86394717.t: The bulb lights when copper is tested but does not light when plastic is tested. What can the student conclude?
tieu_chi: Says copper is an electrical conductor (lets electricity flow).
Says plastic is an electrical insulator (does not let electricity flow).
mau: Copper is an electrical conductor and plastic is an electrical insulator.

b.5915746c.yeu_cau: PART 3: THINKING QUESTIONS (LEVEL 3) Answer the questions in full sentences.
b.5915746c.t: You are given four unknown substances A, B, C and D. You test their properties and record the results in the table. Use the information to identify which substance is most likely to be a metal.
tieu_chi: Names substance B.
Explains using the table: B conducts electricity and is attracted to a magnet (it is also hard and does not dissolve), like a metal such as iron.
Use your own science knowledge.
mau: Substance B is most likely to be a metal. It conducts electricity and is attracted to a magnet, like iron. It is also hard and does not dissolve in water.
Substance A could also be a metal such as copper, but B is also attracted to a magnet, so B is the more certain choice.
b.5915746c.bai_doc:
Results

Substance | Magnetic (attracted to magnet) | Conducts electricity | Soluble in water | Hardness
A | No | Yes | No | Hard
B | Yes | Yes | No | Hard
C | No | No | Yes | Soft
D | No | No | Yes | Hard
Explain your answer.

b.5838c80a.yeu_cau: Answer each question about mass and weight.
b.5838c80a.t: Name the instrument used to measure mass.
tieu_chi: Names a balance or a scale (a weighing scale). A short phrase is enough.
mau: A balance or scale

b.1837c21e.yeu_cau: Answer each question about mass and weight.
b.1837c21e.t: Name the units mass is measured in.
tieu_chi: Names both grams and kilograms (g and kg), in any order. A short phrase is enough.
mau: Grams (g) and kilograms (kg)

b.427831ee.t: Compare the rover's weight on Earth and on the Moon. Why are the two numbers different even though the rover's mass never changed?
tieu_chi: Compares the two weights: the rover weighs more on Earth (50 N) than on the Moon (8 N).
Explains why: gravity on the Moon is weaker than on Earth; weight depends on gravity, while the mass stays the same.
mau: On Earth the rover weighs 50 N, but on the Moon it weighs only 8 N. The numbers are different because gravity on the Moon is much weaker than on Earth. Weight depends on gravity, but the mass stays 5 kg.
b.427831ee.bai_doc:
Gravity Factors

Weight (N) = Mass (kg) × Gravity (N/kg)
Gravity (N/kg): Earth 10 · Moon 1.6 · Mars 3.7 · Jupiter 24.8

b.610b497b.yeu_cau: Look back at questions 1 and 2. Both objects have a net force of 0 N.
b.610b497b.t: What does a net force of 0 N tell you about how the object will move? Explain in your own words.
tieu_chi: Explains that the motion does not change: a still object stays still, or a moving object keeps the same speed and direction. One of these is enough.
Saying the forces are balanced (they cancel each other out) is a bonus, not required.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: A net force of 0 N means the forces are balanced. The object's motion does not change: if it is still, it stays still, like the rope in the tug-of-war; if it is moving, it keeps moving at the same speed, like the falling leaf.

b.17762f27.t: A classmate says, "It doesn't matter how long I draw the arrows — a force is a force." In your own words, explain what the length of an arrow shows and why getting it wrong changes what the diagram says about the object's motion.
tieu_chi: Says the length of an arrow shows the size (strength) of the force: a longer arrow means a bigger force.
Explains why it matters: arrows of the wrong length can make the forces look balanced when they are unbalanced (or the other way round), so the diagram shows the wrong motion.
mau: The length of an arrow shows the size of the force: a longer arrow means a bigger force. If the arrows are the wrong length, the diagram can show balanced forces when they are really unbalanced (or the other way round), so it shows the wrong motion.

b.3afffe8c.yeu_cau: Use the words in the Word Bank to help you answer the questions below.
b.3afffe8c.t: Write a scientific question for Maya's investigation:
tieu_chi: Asks how the surface (how smooth or rough it is) affects how far the toy car rolls.
It is a question that a test can answer. A short sentence is enough.
mau: How does the type of surface affect how far the toy car rolls?
b.3afffe8c.bai_doc:
Part 1: Toy Car on Different Surfaces

Maya pushes the same toy car down the same ramp three times. First the ramp ends on smooth tiles, then on carpet, then on rough concrete. Each time she measures how far the car rolls. She always releases the car from the same point at the top of the ramp.

b.444cbf3d.yeu_cau: Use the words in the Word Bank to help you answer the questions below.
b.444cbf3d.t: Write a scientific question for Omani's investigation using this sentence stem:
tieu_chi: Asks how the mass of the block affects the force needed to pull it.
It is a question that a test can answer. A short sentence is enough.
mau: How does the mass of the block affect the force needed to pull it?
b.444cbf3d.bai_doc:
Part 2: Pulling Objects with Different Masses

Omani ties a string to a wooden block and pulls it across a desk with a force meter. He repeats the test with blocks of different masses: 100 g, 200 g, and 300 g. He uses the same desk, the same string, and the same force meter each time, and he records the force needed to pull each block.

b.12df5c44.yeu_cau: Use the words in the Word Bank to help you answer the questions below.
b.12df5c44.t: Write a scientific question for Priya's investigation using this sentence stem:
tieu_chi: Asks how the number of weights affects how much the elastic band stretches.
It is a question that a test can answer. A short sentence is enough.
mau: How does the number of weights affect how much the elastic band stretches?
b.12df5c44.bai_doc:
Part 3: Stretching Elastic Bands

Priya hangs different numbers of weights from the same elastic band. She uses 1 weight, then 2 weights, then 3 weights. Each time she measures how much longer the elastic band stretches. She hangs the weights the same way and uses the same type of weight every time.

b.92273a08.yeu_cau: Look back at all three investigations.
b.92273a08.t: Explain why keeping the controlled variables the same makes each one a fair test.
tieu_chi: Says that only one thing (the independent variable) is changed and everything else is kept the same.
Explains why this is fair: any change in the results must be caused by that one thing.
The idea may come from the learner's own science knowledge; it does not have to be written in the text.
mau: Keeping the controlled variables the same means only the independent variable changes. Then any change in the results must be caused by that one thing, so the test is fair.

b.337942e3.yeu_cau: Part 5: Reading Graphs — Increase or Decrease?
b.337942e3.t: Look at Graph 1 again. If Maya tested the car on an even rougher surface, would you expect the distance rolled to increase or decrease? Explain your answer.
tieu_chi: Predicts that the distance rolled would decrease.
Explains using the pattern in Graph 1: the rougher the surface, the shorter the distance. Mentioning more friction is a bonus, not required.
mau: I would expect the distance rolled to decrease. Graph 1 shows that the rougher the surface, the shorter the distance the car rolls, so an even rougher surface should give an even shorter distance.

b.e71362b5.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
tieu_chi: Says the heart pumps blood around the body. Adding why this matters (blood carries oxygen or food, keeps us alive) is a bonus, not required.
mau: The heart is important because it pumps blood around the whole body, and the blood carries oxygen to all our cells.

b.8afb2a48.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.8afb2a48.t: What is the function of lungs? ___
tieu_chi: Says the lungs take in air / let us breathe, and oxygen passes from the air into the blood. Mentioning carbon dioxide being breathed out is a bonus, not required.
mau: The lungs take air into the body. Oxygen from the air moves into the blood in the lungs, and carbon dioxide leaves the blood and is breathed out.

b.f5407f6f.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.f5407f6f.t: Your body has several ways to defend itself against pathogens, such as ___
tieu_chi: Names at least two defences: skin as a barrier, white blood cells attacking germs, vaccines training the immune system (others like mucus, tears or stomach acid are also correct).
mau: Your body has several ways to defend itself against pathogens, such as the skin, which acts as a barrier, and white blood cells, which attack germs. Vaccines also train the immune system to fight pathogens.

b.c3e2ed8a.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.c3e2ed8a.t: Washing your hands helps stop diseases from spreading because ___
tieu_chi: Says soap / washing removes or kills germs (pathogens) on the hands, so they cannot get into the body or spread.
mau: Washing your hands helps stop diseases from spreading because soap removes germs from your hands before they can get into your body or onto other people.

b.a6b6db3f.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.a6b6db3f.t: Malaria is caused by a parasite and spread by mosquito bites. People can protect themselves from being infected by ___
tieu_chi: Gives at least one correct way to avoid mosquito bites or reduce mosquitoes: mosquito nets, insect repellent, long sleeves, removing still water, insecticide. Medicine or a vaccine is also acceptable.
mau: People can protect themselves from being infected by sleeping under a mosquito net, using insect repellent and getting rid of still water where mosquitoes breed.

b.90d6b55b.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.90d6b55b.t: List three good hygiene habits that help stop the spread of disease, and explain how each one works. ___
tieu_chi: Lists three different good hygiene habits (for example hand washing, covering coughs and sneezes, not sharing towels or bottles, keeping wounds clean and covered, keeping the body clean).
Explains how each habit stops germs / pathogens spreading. Each habit needs a short explanation; one short phrase each is enough.
mau: 1. Wash your hands with soap: it removes germs before they get into your body. 2. Cover your mouth when you cough or sneeze: it stops droplets full of pathogens landing on people. 3. Do not share towels or water bottles: germs cannot pass from one person to another.

b.47150df9.yeu_cau: What evidence of chemical change do you see? Write «no evidence» if there is none.
tieu_chi: Says there is no evidence of chemical change (no new substance is made). Saying «none» or «no evidence» is enough.
mau: There is no evidence of chemical change. No new substance is made; the water can be frozen back into ice.

b.1e743e84.yeu_cau: What evidence of chemical change do you see? Write «no evidence» if there is none.
tieu_chi: Names at least one piece of evidence: colour change, gas bubbles (the cake rises), a new smell, or a new substance is made.
mau: The colour changes to brown, gas bubbles make the cake rise, and a new substance (the cake) is made.

b.6960c560.yeu_cau: What evidence of chemical change do you see? Write «no evidence» if there is none.
b.6960c560.t: Bread toasting until it turns brown. Evidence: ___
tieu_chi: Names the colour change (the bread turns brown). A new smell or a new substance being made is also acceptable.
mau: The bread changes colour to brown, so a new substance is made.

b.d9b7d178.yeu_cau: What evidence of chemical change do you see? Write «no evidence» if there is none.
b.d9b7d178.t: Stirring sugar into warm water. Evidence: ___
tieu_chi: Says there is no evidence of chemical change (the sugar only dissolves, no new substance). Saying «none» or «no evidence» is enough.
mau: There is no evidence of chemical change. The sugar dissolves but it is still sugar; we can get it back by evaporating the water.

b.3b7dd419.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.3b7dd419.t: You have two clear liquids. Liquid A boils at 100°C and Liquid B boils at 78°C. I could identify each liquid by ___
tieu_chi: Says to heat the liquids and measure / find the temperature at which each one boils (its boiling point).
Links the result to the liquid: the one that boils at 100°C is A (water), at 78°C is B; or says each substance has its own boiling point.
mau: I could identify each liquid by heating them and measuring the temperature at which each one boils. The one that boils at 100°C is Liquid A and the one that boils at 78°C is Liquid B, because every substance has its own boiling point.

b.344075c7.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.344075c7.t: A puddle dries up on a warm day without bubbling. This is evaporation, not boiling, because ___
tieu_chi: Says the water changes to gas only at the surface, slowly, or at a temperature lower than its boiling point.
Contrasts with boiling (fast, bubbles throughout, at the boiling point) OR uses the clue that there are no bubbles. One of these is enough.
mau: This is evaporation, not boiling, because the water turns into a gas slowly, only at the surface, and below its boiling point. Boiling would be fast, with bubbles all through the water, at 100°C.

b.d21ef79f.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.d21ef79f.t: Use the particle model to explain what happens to the sugar particles when sugar dissolves in water. ___
tieu_chi: Says the sugar particles separate / are pulled apart (by the water particles).
Says the sugar particles spread out and mix (evenly) among the water particles; they are still there, not destroyed. Either idea completes this point.
mau: The water particles bump into the sugar particles and pull them apart. The sugar particles spread out and mix evenly among the water particles. The sugar seems to disappear, but its particles are still there.

b.1b279c14.yeu_cau: Give one example of a chemical reaction. Name the reactants and the products.
tieu_chi: Gives a real chemical reaction (for example baking a cake, burning wood, toasting bread, frying an egg, rusting iron, vinegar and baking soda).
Names at least one reactant or the product correctly for that reaction.
mau: When a cake bakes, the reactants are flour, eggs and sugar, and the product is the cake.

b.52fd58d7.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.52fd58d7.t: A book resting on a table does not move. This is because the forces on it are balanced, which means ___
tieu_chi: Says EITHER that the forces are equal in size and act in opposite directions (they cancel out), OR that the object stays still / keeps moving at the same speed because the forces do not change its motion. Either idea is enough; naming gravity and the table pushing up is a bonus.
mau: The forces on it are balanced, which means they are the same size but push or pull in opposite directions: gravity pulls the book down and the table pushes it up just as much, so its motion does not change.

b.9a7edfd0.yeu_cau: Explain Your Thinking — Finish each sentence stem in your own words.
b.9a7edfd0.t: When you ride a bike downhill, you speed up without pedaling. The unbalanced force causing this is ___
tieu_chi: Names gravity as the force.
Explains it is bigger than the forces slowing the bike (friction, air resistance) OR that it pulls the bike down the hill so it speeds up. One of these is enough.
mau: The unbalanced force causing this is gravity. Gravity pulls the bike down the hill more strongly than friction and air resistance hold it back, so the bike speeds up.

b.c3672be1.yeu_cau: Use the names of forces to explain.
b.c3672be1.t: Why does a boat float on a lake? ___
tieu_chi: Names upthrust (the water pushing up on the boat).
Says upthrust balances / is as big as gravity (the weight) pulling down. Saying the forces are balanced is enough.
mau: The water pushes up on the boat with upthrust. The upthrust balances the gravity pulling the boat down, so the boat floats.

b.1d5c3323.yeu_cau: Use the names of forces to explain.
b.1d5c3323.t: Why does a skydiver fall more slowly when the parachute opens? ___
tieu_chi: Says air resistance becomes bigger because the parachute is large / catches more air.
Says air resistance pushes up against gravity pulling down, so the skydiver slows down or falls slowly.
mau: The big parachute catches a lot of air, so the air resistance pushing up becomes much bigger. The skydiver slows down until air resistance balances gravity, and then falls slowly at a steady speed.

b.32954544.yeu_cau: Is it a fair test? Explain, and say how to make it fair.
b.32954544.t: Sam wants to find out which ball bounces highest. He drops a tennis ball from 1 metre and a football from 2 metres. ___
tieu_chi: Says it is not fair because the drop height is different (two things change).
Says how to fix it: drop both balls from the same height.
mau: It is not a fair test because Sam changes two things: the type of ball and the height he drops it from. To make it fair, he should drop both balls from the same height, for example 1 metre.

b.768006ac.yeu_cau: Is it a fair test? Explain, and say how to make it fair.
b.768006ac.t: Lan wants to find out if sugar dissolves faster in hot water or cold water. She puts one spoon of sugar in hot water and three spoons of sugar in cold water. ___
tieu_chi: Says it is not fair because the amount of sugar is different.
Says how to fix it: use the same amount of sugar (and the same amount of water); only the temperature changes.
mau: It is not a fair test because she uses a different amount of sugar in each glass. To make it fair, she should use the same amount of sugar, for example one spoon in each glass, and only change the temperature of the water.

b.9fa7007a.yeu_cau: Is it a fair test? Explain, and say how to make it fair.
b.9fa7007a.t: Tom wants to find out if a toy car rolls further on carpet or on tiles. He pushes the car hard on the tiles and gently on the carpet. ___
tieu_chi: Says it is not fair because the push (force) is different.
Says how to fix it: give the same push each time, for example roll the car down the same ramp from the same height.
mau: It is not a fair test because he pushes the car with a different force each time. To make it fair, he should let the car roll down the same ramp from the same height on both surfaces, so only the surface changes.

b.15af5ad3.yeu_cau: Is it a fair test? Explain, and say how to make it fair.
b.15af5ad3.t: In a fair test, how many things should you change on purpose? Why? ___
tieu_chi: Says only one thing (the independent variable) should change.
Explains that otherwise you cannot tell which change caused the result.
mau: You should change only one thing on purpose. If you change more than one thing, you cannot tell which change caused the result.

b.085a07dc.yeu_cau: Mastery Check — the questions you explain in your own words.
b.085a07dc.t: Maya wants to find out if jumping jacks raise pulse rate more than walking. She measures her pulse after jumping jacks, then measures her friend's pulse after walking, and compares the two numbers. Why is Maya's investigation not a fair test? Name the problem and explain how she could fix it. ___
tieu_chi: Names the problem: two different people are measured (Maya and her friend), so more than one thing changes.
Says how to fix it: the same person does both activities (and keeps other things the same, e.g. the same time, resting between trials).
mau: It is not a fair test because Maya measures her own pulse after jumping jacks but her friend's pulse after walking, so two things change: the person and the exercise. She could fix it by measuring her own pulse after both activities, doing each one for the same time and resting in between.

b.c719eb98.yeu_cau: Mastery Check — the questions you explain in your own words.
b.c719eb98.t: Look at the bar chart. A student has an unlabeled liquid that boils at about 102°C. Use the chart to identify which substance it most likely is, and explain how the boiling point helped you decide. ___
tieu_chi: Identifies salt water.
Explains using the chart: salt water boils at 103°C, closest to 102°C (or each substance has its own boiling point). Saying water is also close is fine if salt water is chosen.
mau: It is most likely salt water. Salt water boils at 103°C, which is the closest to 102°C. Each substance has its own boiling point, so we can use it to identify a liquid.

b.099628ad.yeu_cau: Mastery Check — the questions you explain in your own words.
b.099628ad.t: Look at the bar chart. A new unknown substance boils at 250°C. Predict whether it is more like the oil or more like the alcohol. Use the pattern in the chart to explain your prediction. ___
tieu_chi: Predicts it is more like the oil.
Explains using the numbers in the chart: 250°C is much closer to oil (300°C) than to alcohol (78°C).
mau: It is more like the oil. Oil boils at 300°C, which is close to 250°C, but alcohol boils at only 78°C, which is very far away.
